nameStory: The black guillemot gets its straightforward name from its striking jet-black summer plumage that makes it unmistakable among seabirds. In some regions, especially Scotland, it's also called a 'tystie' - a delightful local name that comes from the Old Norse word meaning 'small bird.'
description: The black guillemot is a medium-sized seabird that belongs to the auk family, the same group as puffins and murres. In summer, these compact diving birds are unmistakable with their coal-black feathers contrasted by bright white wing patches and coral-red feet. During winter, they transform into pale gray and white birds with a subtle barred pattern on their backs. They're expert underwater hunters, using their wings to 'fly' beneath the surface while chasing fish and crustaceans.

idTips.label: Wing patches
idTips.description: Large, brilliant white patches on the upper wings create a bold contrast against the black summer plumage - these patches are visible both in flight and when the bird is swimming

idTips.label: Feet color
idTips.description: Bright coral-red or orange-red webbed feet that seem almost glowing against dark rocks or water - much more vivid than most seabirds

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Long, slender black bill that looks almost needle-like compared to the thick, chunky bills of puffins or murres

idTips.label: Winter plumage
idTips.description: In winter, transforms to pale gray above with white below, showing a distinctive barred pattern on the back and shoulders that looks almost scaly

idTips.label: Swimming behavior
idTips.description: Often seen floating alone or in small groups near rocky shores, frequently diving completely underwater and popping up unexpectedly elsewhere

habitat: Black guillemots favor rocky coastlines, especially around cliffs, boulder fields, and offshore islands along New England's coast. You'll most often spot them in the waters near Maine's rocky shores, around places like Acadia National Park or the offshore islands. They prefer areas where they can nest in cliff crevices or gaps between large rocks above the high tide line.

seasonality.spring: Breeding birds arrive in their striking black plumage with white wing patches, often seen near rocky nesting sites from late February through May. This is when their coral-red feet are most vibrant.
seasonality.summer: Peak viewing season with birds in full black breeding plumage, actively diving for fish near shore. Adults may be seen carrying small fish crosswise in their bills back to hidden chicks in rock crevices.
seasonality.fall: Birds begin molting into winter plumage, showing a patchy mix of black and gray-white feathers. Some northern populations start moving south during this transition period.
seasonality.winter: Most birds appear in pale gray and white winter plumage with distinctive barred backs. Arctic populations join year-round residents, making this the best time to see larger numbers along New England coasts.

funFact: Black guillemot chicks are born covered in fluffy black down and are fed whole fish delivered headfirst - but when they're ready to fledge at just 5-6 weeks old, their parents completely abandon them, forcing the youngsters to figure out ocean life entirely on their own with no parental guidance whatsoever.
confusionNotes: In winter plumage, black guillemots can be confused with other small seabirds, but remember the 'barred back' - that distinctive gray and white striped pattern on their shoulders and back is like a winter ID badge that no other New England seabird shares.
contextualKnowledge: While called 'black' guillemot, these birds spend nearly half the year in gray-and-white winter plumage, so don't expect to always see a black bird. The dramatic seasonal color change is one of the most striking transformations among New England seabirds.
compareHints: Black guillemots are the only true guillemots regularly seen in New England waters. Compared to their auk relatives, they're smaller and more slender than murres, lack the colorful facial features of puffins, and are the only ones with those distinctive white wing patches. Their coral-red feet are also much brighter than the orange or yellow feet of other auks.
